Strike by Construction Materials Workers Disrupts Japanese Supply Chains

A widespread walkout by workers in Japan’s construction materials industry entered its third day on Tuesday, causing significant disruptions to the delivery and production of cement, rebar, and aggregates, according to industry groups and company representatives.

The strike began early Sunday morning after wage negotiations between the All-Japan Construction Materials Workers Union and the employers’ association broke down. Workers at plants and distribution centers operated by major firms such as Nihon Materials and Sakura Cement have halted production and deliveries, impacting construction sites nationwide.

Industry analysts estimate that as much as 60% of Japan’s domestic cement production capacity is currently offline. “We are seeing immediate ripple effects at building sites where concrete pours and structural work are scheduled,” said Hideki Yamamoto, senior analyst at the Tokyo Construction Research Institute. “Even a short disruption can cause delays across multiple projects.”

The union is demanding a 7% wage increase and improved overtime benefits, citing rising living costs and long hours. “Our members have kept this industry going through difficult times,” said union leader Takashi Mori at a press conference in Osaka. “We are committed to negotiating, but we need our concerns to be taken seriously.”

Employers have so far offered a 2.5% raise, which they say reflects current economic conditions. A spokesperson for the Construction Materials Producers Association said, “We recognize the importance of our workforce and are continuing discussions to reach a fair solution as soon as possible.”

Trade groups warn that the ongoing strike could lead to further shortages of essential materials if not resolved quickly. The Japan Ready-Mix Concrete Association reported delivery volumes down by more than half since the walkout began. “If the stoppage continues for several more days, inventory levels at job sites could run critically low,” said association president Masaru Suzuki.

Negotiations between union representatives and management are set to resume later this week.
